---
title: "Subagents, Agent Skills, and MCP"
---

In this episode we're going to go a little deeper with coding agents by learning
how to customize their functionality through advanced features. Subagents, Agent
Skills, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) all represent ways to extend what
a coding agent can do beyond its default configuration — delegating work to
other agents, packaging reusable expertise, and connecting to external tools
and data sources.

Before getting into these topic, let's take a moment to better understand the
anatomy of a coding agents session. Even before you enter your first prompt in a
new OpenCode session, the session already includes a lot of information, such as:

- **System prompt** — instructions from the agent's developers that define its
  role, behavior, and constraints. (e.g. "You are opencode, an interactive CLI agent specializing in software engineering tasks. Your primary goal is to ...").
- **Tool definitions** — descriptions of the tools available to the agent (reading
  and editing files, running shell commands, fetching web pages, etc.) and
  guidance on when to use them.
- **Project context** — files like `AGENTS.md` (see the previous episode) that
  are read automatically so the agent starts out already familiar with your
  project's conventions and structure.


## Subagents

A subagent is a separate agent instance created by the main AI coding agent to
handle a specific task. Subagents have their own **system prompts** and they run
in a separate context, not in the main conversation thread.


The subagent will start in a new session with its own context window, receive
instructions from the agent, complete the task, and return a summary to the main
session that spawned the subagent. This is another advantage of the subagent: it
won't overload your current chat session with all the analysis and process, it
will only return a summary when the task is completed.

:::{.callout-tip}
### Exploring System Prompts

OpenCode includes a few pre-configured subagents called **Explore** and
**General**. We can learn about these subagents by reading their system prompts.

Start a new session try the following prompts in succession.

1. `Print the first few sentences of your system prompt`
2. `@general Print the first few sentences of your system prompt`
3. `@explore Print the first few sentences of your system prompt`

:::

## Agent Skills

Agent Skills are a way to encapsulate and distribute specialized knowledge or
workflows for agents. The core specification is described at
[https://agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io).

A minimal Agent Skill consists of a directory with a file, `SKILL.md` that
includes some metadata (a `name` and `description` in the file's front-matter)
and some content in the body of the file. 

For example, here is a portion of the `SKILL.md` file from an Agent Skill
describing how to make best of use of the Coder Workspace environment. (The
[full text is available on GitHub](https://github.com/ucsb-dreamlab/skill)).


```md
---
name: dreamlab-coder-workspace
description: Use features of the DREAM Lab Coder Workspace Environment
---

You are running in an Ubuntu-based virtual machine with sudo access. 

[etc..]

```

### Installing a Skill

Like many coding agent configurations, you can install Agent Skills in either a
project-specific or global configuration directory. (See OpenCode's [Agent
Skills documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/skills/)).

We will use the following: 
- Project agent-compatible: `.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`
- Global agent-compatible: `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`
